title: A translational tile with no periodic tiling in dimension three
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: An exposition of OpenAI's proof (2026) that the periodic tiling conjecture fails in dimension three: there is a finite set T in Z^3 that tiles Z^3 by translations, but no tiling set is invariant under a subgroup of finite index, and the union of the closed unit cubes with lower corners in T tiles R^3 almost everywhere, but no tiling set is invariant under a lattice of full rank, even with arbitrary real translations. The first lesson sets up tilings of abelian groups, periods and the passage to R^d, and proves Newman's theorem that tilings of Z by one finite tile are periodic. The second proves that no array with the two-digit p-adic Sudoku rule of Greenfeld and Tao and no constant column has a vertical period, and that the last-nonzero-digit array obeys the rule. The third encodes symbols as the dependence of outputs on input digits through tiling equations in Z^2 x V with V finite and cyclic: a graph equation, invariance tiles and cycle tests. The fourth forces activity with a nonuniform shift list and shows that a fully periodic common solution would give a vertically periodic array. The fifth constructs one common solution from labelled blocks and seed regions sharing one output. The sixth stacks the system into one tile in Z^2 x Z/Q with a fresh prime. The seventh builds the tile of Z^3 from a rigid transversal with a marked cube and shows that periodic tilings of R^3 have grid centers and descend to Z^2 x Z/Q.
prerequisites: core course Abstract Algebra I (Judson, Abstract Algebra: Theory and Applications): Bezout's identity (Corollary 2.2.3), infinitely many primes (Theorem 2.2.6), orders of elements divide the order of a finite group (Corollary 6.2.3), products of cyclic groups of coprime orders (Theorem 9.2.9, Corollary 9.2.10), the Chinese remainder theorem (Theorem 16.5.3)
core course Linear Algebra (Hefferon, Linear Algebra, fourth edition): in an n-dimensional space n linearly independent vectors span (Chapter Two, Section III, Corollary 2.14)
core course Measure and Integration (Fremlin, Measure Theory, Volume 1): countable additivity (112C), Borel sets and the measure of boxes (115G), translation invariance (134A)
finite probability spaces: independence and the union bound

checks.reading: The manuscript 'A translational tile with no fully periodic tiling in dimension three' (OpenAI, 23 Sep 2026; paper.tex with the main theorem, introduction 97 lines, word rule 295, cyclic encoding 329, activation 357, common solution 338, stacking 131, three dimensions 400, two figures, references.bib; one edition in the release, listing at commit 1581d4cb) was read in full on 15 Oct 2026, and every step was derived again while the lessons were written: the allowed words and their dependence on the residues of the witness modulo p^2; the count of squares without exceptional cells and the choice of K; the second differences along the diagonals of the square; the spreading of good cells along lines and rows; vertical nondegeneracy; the normalization and rescaling in the obstruction and the contradiction for B_1 = 0; the last-nonzero-digit model and the line maps; the choice of primes and the cyclicity of V; the graph equation and the sheared coordinates; invariance tiles; active labels; the cycle test and its bijection criterion in both directions; the shift list mu = 1 + omega and its fibre orderings; batches, the activation tiles and their sizes; the fibre criterion; ordinary and seed activation, including the integer decomposition Q = u + v; the extraction of the array and the vertical period from a finite-index period group; labelled blocks and the block inverse; the seed regions, label spaces and the shared output; the inverse of both seed tests; the compatibility of all equations; the partition with full difference sets; stacking in both directions; the rigid transversal; the tile T and its disjointness; existence of tilings; rounding in the closed box; grid centers; kernel invariance and descent. No error found. Additions in the course: a proof of Newman's theorem with the forward and backward rules; the observation, with an example, that for Z x G0 not every tiling set is periodic, while some tiling set is (exercise); elementary lemmas on subgroups of Z^d and on thickenings; an explicit multiplicity formula for invariance tiles; the proof that the form of the affine approximation is unique (exercise); a sharper probability bound (4/25)^3 in the rigid-representatives lemma, since the needed differences lie in {-1, 0, 1}; and a proof by a segment and least elements, in place of the connectedness of R^3, that the centers of a periodic assembly lie in one coset. The Lean formalization in the release (scope note lean/docs/155.md, comparator statement PeriodicTilingThree.lean, 122 files in OAI/Geometry/PeriodicTiling, none containing sorry) states the main theorem together with the minimality of dimension three; it was not built or run. open_obligations: The planar theorem (every finite tile of Z^2 has a fully periodic tiling set; Bhattacharya 2020, Greenfeld-Tao 2021), which together with Newman's theorem makes three the least dimension for lattice tilings, is stated with free references in the first lesson and not proved in the course; it is not used in the proof of the main theorem. OpenAI's Lean formalization includes a proof of it.
The lessons were written and checked by one model in one session; they have not been checked by a second reader.
